record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.original_question: How should Wolf-Rayet spectral classifications be mapped to the underlying stellar structures, evolutionary states, and feedback properties of Wolf-Rayet stars? The answer must account for the fact that the same WN, WC, or WO subtype label can be produced by line ratios with different absolute line strengths, kinetic feedback, hydrostatic radii, hydrogen content, and burning stages, so treating Wolf-Rayet stars as one homogeneous group can misrepresent both evolution and feedback.

evidence.quote: However, this does not apply to all WR stars and the treatment of WR stars as one big homogeneous group is another example, where a blurred perception can have striking consequences. The spectral classification into WN, WC, and WO with further subtypes defined by line ratios provides a first distinction, but the association with both evolution and feedback is tricky.

As the ratio of two strong lines can be the same as the ratio of two weaker lines, objects with very different kinetic feedback as well as different hydrostatic radii can appear under the same label. The association with stellar structure and evolution through the subtypes is therefore non-trivial with many pitfalls.

Strong constraints exist for WC and WO stars, which never show hydrogen (H) in their spectra and thus have to be He-burning (“classical”) WR (cWR) stars. WN stars instead can either be H- or He-burning, unless their outer layers are (almost) depleted in H.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are massive, hot, evolved stars characterized by strong, broad emission lines arising in dense, fast stellar winds. They are spectroscopically classified into three principal types based on dominant emission features: WN stars (nitrogen-dominated emission), WC stars (carbon-dominated emission), and WO stars (oxygen-dominated emission). Each type is further divided into subtypes (e.g., WN2–WN11, WC4–WC9, WO1–WO4) defined by ratios of specific emission line strengths. Physically, WC and WO stars never display hydrogen in their spectra and must therefore be helium-burning ("classical") WR stars, while WN stars may be either hydrogen-burning or helium-burning depending on their hydrogen content. Two stars with very different absolute line strengths, mass-loss rates, terminal wind velocities, kinetic feedback into the interstellar medium, hydrostatic (core) radii, surface hydrogen mass fraction X_H, and current nuclear burning stage can produce identical line ratios and therefore share the same subtype label.

Construct an explicit, well-defined mapping

  Φ : {WR spectral subtype labels} ⟶ 𝒮,

where 𝒮 is a space of physical descriptors of the form

  s = (M_*, R_hydro, L_*, T_eff, Ṁ, v_∞, X_H, burning stage, evolutionary phase, Ė_kin),

(stellar mass, hydrostatic radius, luminosity, effective temperature at the hydrostatic radius, mass-loss rate, wind terminal velocity, surface hydrogen fraction, the current core nuclear burning stage, the evolutionary phase, and the wind kinetic-energy feedback rate Ė_kin = ½ Ṁ v_∞²), such that Φ is consistent with the observed degeneracies (different absolute line strengths can yield identical line ratios). Determine to what extent Φ can be made single-valued, identify the multivalued regions, and characterize the fibers Φ⁻¹(label) — that is, the full set of physically distinct stellar structures, evolutionary states, and feedback properties that can hide behind a single WN, WC, or WO subtype designation.
artifact.status_search_result: The classification-to-physics mapping for Wolf-Rayet stars remains an open problem in massive-star astrophysics. Recent reviews and modeling work (e.g., Sander, Crowther, Shenar and collaborators) emphasize that WR subtypes do not uniquely determine stellar structure, hydrogen content, evolutionary phase, or kinetic feedback, and ongoing efforts using PoWR/CMFGEN atmosphere models continue to refine but not resolve the degeneracies.

status_evidence.title: The Wolf-Rayet stars in the Magellanic Clouds (Shenar et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Spectral subtypes of WR stars do not map uniquely to evolutionary status; hydrogen content and luminosity vary substantially within subtypes.
status_evidence.claim: Mapping from WR subtype to physical state is non-unique, supporting open status.

status_evidence.title: Sander, A.A.C., review on Wolf-Rayet winds
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses persistent uncertainties in connecting WR spectral appearance to mass-loss, hydrostatic radii, and evolutionary stage.
status_evidence.claim: Connection between WR classification and physics remains an active open question.
